question: On a low-voltage power breaker, ATS 7.6.1.2 lists long-time, short-time, ground-fault, and instantaneous pickup as primary-injection tests. Secondary injection is:
choices: Required before any primary test
Marked optional, and it is not the method named for those four pickup tests
The only acceptable method for electronic trip units
Prohibited by NEMA AB 4
explanation: B.3 through B.6 say determine those functions by primary current injection. B.7, secondary injection, carries the optional asterisk. Secondary injection does not pass current through the sensors and the poles.

question: Which item is an electrical test in ATS 7.6.1.2, not a visual and mechanical inspection item?
choices: Compare the nameplate with the drawings
Contact / pole resistance
Verify tightness of bolted connections
Confirm settings match the coordination study
explanation: Contact resistance is in the electrical-test list (B.2), with its limit in D.2. Nameplate comparison, torque, and the coordination-study settings check sit in the visual and mechanical section. NETA wording traps hang on that split.

question: No manufacturer curve is available. A molded-case breaker rated 100 A, 480 V, is tested at 300% of continuous rating. Table 100.7 maximum trip time is:
explanation: The 51–100 A row and the 251–600 V column is 160 seconds. The ≤250 V column on that row is 140 seconds. 50 seconds is the 0–30 A, ≤250 V cell. The table is specifically the 300% test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.7; Table 100.7 note 1 (derived from NEMA AB 4-2017, Table 3)

question: Control-wiring insulation resistance on a low-voltage power breaker shall not be less than:
choices: 2 MΩ
25 MΩ
100 MΩ
500 MΩ
explanation: ATS 7.6.1.2.D.3 states 2 MΩ for control wiring. The 100 MΩ figure is the Table 100.1 floor for 600 V power insulation, not the control-wire floor.

question: Which auxiliary feature does ATS 7.6.1.2.B.8 tell you to verify on a low-voltage power breaker?
choices: Zone interlocking
Oil dielectric strength
Turns ratio of the power transformer
Wenner soil resistivity
explanation: The list includes trip and pickup indicators, zone interlocking, electrical close and trip, trip-free, antipump, and the trip-unit battery. Oil tests, TTR, and soil boxes are other sections.

question: Trip-free operation means:
choices: The breaker cannot trip while a lockout relay is picked up
The breaker will trip even if the close command is held
The closing spring will recharge while the trip coil is energized
Antipump has been defeated on purpose
explanation: Trip-free is the ability to trip even if close is held, so a fault during a close still opens the breaker. Antipump is the separate function that prevents a second close until the close signal is removed and reasserted. ATS tells you to verify both; it does not define them in that sentence. The definitions are the mechanism behavior.

question: Adjustable instantaneous trip, field tolerance. ATS-2025 Table 100.8 versus MTS-2023 Table 100.8:
choices: Both are +40% / −40%
Both are +25% / −25% of the setting
explanation: Electronic trip units are +30% / −30% in both tables. Adjustable units are ±40% in ATS-2025 and +40% / −30% in MTS-2023. The ±25% figures apply to nonadjustable breakers, measured outside the published band, not to the adjustable setting.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.8; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.8

question: An electronic trip unit's instantaneous setting is tested in the field with no manufacturer tolerance in hand. Which band applies in both ATS-2025 and MTS-2023 Table 100.8?
choices: +25% outside the printed band
explanation: Electronic trip units are +30% and −30% of the setting in both tables. The adjustable +40% row is a different breaker type. Putting the adjustable band on an electronic unit is the table miss.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.8; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.8

question: Table 100.12.1, cadmium- or zinc-plated steel, 1/2 inch SAE grade 5. Torque is:
choices: 30 lb-ft
48 lb-ft
74 lb-ft
20 lb-ft
explanation: Grade 5, 1/2 inch, is 48 pound-feet. Grade 1 and 2 at that diameter are 30. Grade 8 is 74. The head mark has to match the column, and metric bolts are not this table.

question: Main-tie-main, both mains closed, tie open, loads split. An operator closes the tie and then opens main A. What did that sequence do to the bus that had been fed by main A?
choices: It de-energized that bus
It kept that bus energized from main B through the tie, provided the tie closed first and stayed closed
It de-energized the main B bus
It automatically transfers the ground relay to the other main
explanation: Order matters. Closing the tie while both mains are still closed briefly parallels the two sources, which is a closed transition. Opening main A after that leaves the former A-bus loads fed from main B through the tie. Main B itself stays closed, so the sequence does not de-energize the main B bus. Many main-tie-main schemes block that parallel with a two-out-of-three interlock, or allow it only under sync-check. Open the tie first, or open main A while the tie is still open, and the A bus goes dark. Confirm the interlocks on the actual schematic before operating.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (main-tie-main operation); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Section 8

question: A key interlock between a grounding switch and the live switch keeps the two from being closed at the same time, so the grounding switch cannot close onto a live bus. Someone cuts a second key to the same code. The scheme:
choices: Still enforces the sequence, because the lock manufacturer registered the code
Is defeated; a spare identical key lets both locks be operated
Becomes stronger, because two keys provide redundancy
Only fails if the key is made of aluminum
explanation: The interlock works because there is one key, so the grounding switch and the live switch cannot both be closed. A duplicate lets an operator release both mechanisms. Key control is part of the procedure. The lock cannot police a second key by itself.

question: Zone-selective interlocking is listed in ATS 7.6.1.2.B.8 as something you verify. In the usual scheme, a restraint signal from the downstream breaker causes the upstream breaker to:
choices: Trip instantly, ignoring its delay
Wait on its delayed setting while the downstream device is expected to clear; with no restraint it may trip on the faster unrestrained time
Block all ground-fault protection permanently
Raise its sensor rating to the frame size
explanation: The standard requires the function test. The logic — downstream restraint holds the upstream short-time or ground element on its longer delay, and loss of restraint releases the faster trip — is the scheme you are proving. Confirm the exact behavior in that trip unit's manual.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8; Eaton Digitrip 1150+ instruction leaflet IL70C1036H06, zone interlocking

question: A single-pole primary shot on a four-pole breaker with residual ground fault will often:
choices: Look like a ground fault and trip the ground element
Prove the long-time band cleanly
Bypass the sensors
Read as a healthy three-phase load
explanation: One pole in and nowhere out is residual current, which is what the ground function is built to see. Run the return through the neutral pole, or raise the ground function the way that manual allows, then put the settings back.
reference: Eaton Digitrip 1150+ instruction leaflet IL70C1036H06, Section 5; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.5

question: The trip-unit manual publishes an instantaneous tolerance. ATS 7.6.1.2 says you:
choices: Ignore the manual and use Table 100.8 anyway
Use the published tolerance; Table 100.8 applies only in the absence of manufacturer data
Average the manual and Table 100.8
Use the long-time 300% table
explanation: Instantaneous pickup shall be as specified and within the manufacturer’s published tolerances. Table 100.8 is the fallback when that data does not exist. A manual that says ±10% is a tighter or different story than the adjustable molded-case band.

question: Short-time timing is short, about a few cycles, and zone-interlock restraint was never jumpered. The likely cause is:
choices: The long-time dial
The element tripped unrestrained because no restraint signal was present
Table 100.7
A failed contact-resistance test
explanation: Without a restraint jumper, short-time and ground are allowed to trip on the fast unrestrained time. That is what the scheme does in service when the downstream breaker is not holding them off. Jumper only for the delayed-band shot, then remove it and restore settings.
reference: Eaton Digitrip 1150+ instruction leaflet IL70C1036H06, zone-interlocking restraint jumper; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8

question: On an Eaton PXR 20/25, the long-delay time dial is defined at:
choices: 1×Ir
6×Ir
The instantaneous pickup
explanation: The protection table in the PXR 20/25 user manual labels long delay time at 6 times Ir. A shot at some other multiple is not that dial unless you are on the published curve. Do not treat a hand-scaled time as the acceptance window.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Long-time memory on a PXR trip unit matters during primary injection because:
choices: It erases the rating plug
Repeated overload shots can stack and change the next trip
It disables ground fault
It sets the frame size
explanation: The PXR manual includes long-time memory so repeated overloads are not ignored. For a string of timing shots, turn that memory off if the manual tells you to, then turn it back on and restore the as-found settings.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Instantaneous pickup on a PXR is a multiple of:
choices: Ir, the long-time pickup
In, the sensor or rating plug
The frame’s interrupting rating
6× the short-time delay
explanation: The PXR protection table lists instantaneous as a multiple of In, while short-time pickup is a multiple of Ir. Mixing In and Ir moves the test current by a lot when the plug is not full frame.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Short-time pickup on a PXR is a multiple of Ir, while instantaneous is a multiple of In. If the plug is 800 A in a 1600 A frame and Ir is 1.0, a 6× short-time pickup is:
choices: 6 A
explanation: Ir = 1.0 × 800 = 800 A. Short-time at 6 × Ir is 4800 A. Instantaneous multiples use In, which on this unit is the plug, 800 A, not the 1600 A frame. Read which symbol the dial says before you set the injection current.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Ground-fault delay on a PXR that is labeled at 0.625 × In means the time dial is defined:
choices: At 0.625 times sensor rating, not at an arbitrary current you happened to inject
At 6 × Ir
At the instantaneous setting
Only when zone interlock is on
explanation: The manual’s ground I²t times are at 0.625 × In. A shot at some other current is a different point on the curve. Confirm that point in the manufacturer’s curve before you fail the trip unit.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Zone interlock is enabled and you are timing the delayed short-time band. The restraint input is open. You should expect:
choices: The full delayed band
A fast, unrestrained trip, so the delayed window will not show until restraint is jumpered
No trip at any current
The long-time dial to change
explanation: No restraint means the downstream device is not holding this one back, which is exactly when the scheme is supposed to be fast. Jumper the restraint the way the manual shows, take the delayed shot, then remove the jumper and restore settings.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions (zone interlock); ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8

question: ATS switch inspection says fuse sizes must agree with:
choices: The largest fuse that fits the clips
The drawings and the coordination study
The cable shield resistance
Table 100.11
explanation: 7.5.1.1 checks fuse size and type against the drawings and the study, and it checks that each fuse is supported and has contact integrity. It does not publish a maximum insulation resistance between fuses. Higher insulation resistance is not a failure.

question: A 0.5 A fuse is going to be checked for continuity. The test current should be:
choices: 10 A, because that is a standard ductor range
Below the fuse rating so the test does not open it
The instantaneous pickup of the breaker ahead of it
500 V dc
explanation: ATS checks fuse support and contact. It does not tell you to push 10 A through a half-amp fuse. Stay under the fuse rating.

question: Antipump, which ATS requires you to prove on a power breaker, means:
choices: The breaker will close and trip repeatedly while the close signal is held
One close attempt for a maintained close signal; it will not hammer
The charging motor is supposed to run continuously
The trip coil is disconnected
explanation: Trip-free means it will trip even if close is held. Antipump means it will not reclose over and over while that close signal stays picked up. ATS 7.6.1.3 tests both, with the breaker in the test position, and the test values say those features shall function as designed. A charging motor that stays hot is a reason to prove this, not a reason to keep holding close.

question: Secondary control checks on a medium-voltage breaker, ATS 7.6.1.3, are made:
choices: With the breaker racked in and closed on the bus
In the test position: close and trip from the control switch, and trip from each protective relay
Only with the trip plugs pulled
By a dissolved-gas sample
explanation: The test position lets you operate the mechanism without putting the breaker on the bus. You also prove charge, trip-free, and antipump. Racking a closed breaker into the gear is what the interlock is there to stop.

question: A closed breaker that will not rack into the switchgear is showing:
choices: A failed trip unit that must be primary-injected on the bus
The racking interlock, which requires the breaker to be open
A bad power-factor set
An oil sample problem
explanation: ATS has you prove interlocks by trying the blocked operation. A closed breaker is not supposed to rack in. Open it, then rack. Do not defeat the interlock to finish the job.

question: Bolt grade is identified in the field by:
choices: Head markings (see the grade row of ATS Table 100.12.1)
Table 100.1
The glove class
The PI minimum
explanation: Bolt grade is read from the marks on the head. ATS-2025 Table 100.12.1 puts a head-marking row with the torque values, so the grade and the torque table sit together. Table 100.1, the glove class, and the polarization-index minimum do not identify bolt grade.

question: ATS 7.5 switch tests measure contact resistance:
choices: Across each switchblade and fuseholder
Only from the fuse to the station ground grid
As a maximum insulation resistance between fuses
With a 10 kV megohmmeter as the only instrument
explanation: The fuseholder and the blade are current-carrying joints. Compare them with similar joints. The section does not set a maximum insulation resistance between fuses. Fuse size still has to match the drawings and the study.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.5 places the inverse-time trip test of a low-voltage breaker at:
choices: 300 percent of rated continuous current
150 percent of the frame size, regardless of the plug
The instantaneous setting only
A dissolved-gas sample
explanation: The maintenance table calls for the inverse-time test at 300 percent of rated continuous current, and it also lists instantaneous. It does not print a trip-time band. That time still comes from the manufacturer or from the NETA table that applies to the test you are actually running.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.4 says low-voltage breakers are operated:
choices: Once, then left alone for the rest of the cycle
At least three times
Only if the instantaneous test fails
By a turns-ratio set
explanation: The servicing table includes operating the breaker at least three times, along with torque and interlock checks. Three operations are not a substitute for the electrical tests in the next table, and they are not a numeric contact-resistance limit.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.4.5 says not to run an overpotential test on:
choices: The power poles of a medium-voltage breaker, ever
Control wiring that is connected to solid-state components
The station ground grid
A transfer-switch mechanical interlock
explanation: Medium-voltage breaker maintenance can include an enhanced overpotential test of the power circuit. Control wiring tied to solid-state parts is excluded from that overpotential test. Follow the manufacturer for those circuits instead of forcing a high-voltage test through the electronics.

question: Chapter 15 of NFPA 70B-2026 splits breaker scope at about:
choices: Low-voltage AC breakers through 1000 V, and medium-voltage AC power breakers above 1000 V through 69 kV
All breakers as one table with one test list
Only breakers above 115 kV
Fuses and network protectors
explanation: Molded-case, insulated-case, and low-voltage power breakers are the AC group at 1000 V and below. Medium-voltage power breakers are the AC group above 1000 V through 69 kV. The two groups do not share one test list. Vacuum wear, oil, and gas condition show up on the medium-voltage inspection, not on a 480 V molded-case breaker.

question: Which test is on the low-voltage breaker list in NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.5 and is not the headline of the medium-voltage list?
choices: Inverse-time trip at 300 percent of rated continuous current
Vacuum-interrupter integrity
Contact timing of a medium-voltage mechanism
Enhanced overpotential of the power circuit
explanation: The low-voltage electrical table includes thermography, contact resistance, insulation resistance, controls, electronic-trip calibration, the 300 percent inverse-time test, and instantaneous. The medium-voltage table instead stresses trip and close, mechanism, vacuum integrity, contact timing, and an enhanced overpotential test. Do not run a molded-case 300 percent shot and call it a vacuum-bottle test.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.5 splits molded-case breaker columns at:
choices: Frames of 225 A and below versus larger frames
A 1000 V versus 69 kV insulation test
Vented versus valve-regulated cells
Online versus offline thermography
explanation: The low-voltage electrical table separates molded-case frames of 225 A and below from larger frames. Both still see the inverse-time test at 300 percent of rated continuous current. The table does not give the seconds. That time is the manufacturer’s, or the NETA table if you are running an acceptance or maintenance test that actually publishes one.

question: Low-voltage power circuit breaker switchgear for a 480 V system (508 V rated maximum) has a 2.2 kV factory power-frequency withstand. The field withstand should not exceed:
choices: 2.2 kV
1.0 kV
3.1 kV
explanation: Field withstand on LV switchgear is limited to 75% of the factory value: 0.75 × 2.2 kV = 1.65 kV. Field tests are mainly for added sections or after major changes, and only on gear that has first been cleaned and put in good condition. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.1.1.B.3 and Table 100.2 note 1; ref. IEEE C37.20.1-2015, 6.5 and Table 1.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.1.1.B.3 and Table 100.2 note 1; ref. IEEE C37.20.1-2015, 6.5 and Table 1

question: Commissioning a lineup with key interlocks, you find spare duplicate keys in the shipping box. What should happen to them?
choices: Destroyed, or kept where only authorized personnel can get them
Hung on the gear next to each lock
Given to every operator
Left in the box with the breaker manuals
explanation: A key interlock works only if one key exists per sequence. Spare keys defeat it, so the guide says to destroy them or lock them away from everyone except authorized people.

question: A drawout LV power breaker has a stored-energy closing spring. What protects against an accidental spring discharge during removal?
choices: Blocking full withdrawal while the spring is charged, blocking the close function first, or discharging the spring automatically during withdrawal
A warning label only
Requiring the breaker to be closed before withdrawal
Grounding the breaker frame
explanation: The mechanism also must not release unless it is fully charged. For removal, the gear either stops full withdrawal while charged, blocks closing, or dumps the stored energy on the way out. Check that during commissioning. Source: IEEE C37.20.1-2015, 7.11.2 item c).

question: During acceptance operational tests on a 600 V network protector, which pair of results shows it is working the way a network protector should?
choices: It closes with voltage on the transformer side only, and it opens when the source feeder breaker is opened
It closes only when both sides are dead, and it stays closed when the feeder opens
It opens on any overcurrent on the secondary grid
It closes only by hand, and trips only by remote command
explanation: The ATS operational checks include verifying that the protector closes with voltage on the transformer side only and that it opens when the source feeder breaker opens. Opening the feeder lets the grid back-feed the transformer, and the protector is supposed to open on that reverse flow. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.8.B.11.

question: Network protector control voltage is rated 125 V. With no tighter manufacturer value, the trip actuator must pick up at no more than:
explanation: The ATS limit for trip actuator minimum pickup is 75% of rated control voltage. 0.75 × 125 V = 93.75 V. The same 75% ceiling applies to the motor control relay pickup and the motor closing voltage. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.8.D.7 to D.9.

question: You measure the three power fuses in a network protector: 110, 118, and 128 µΩ. Per the acceptance limits, you should:
choices: Accept them, since all fuses are within 50% of each other
Investigate, because 128 is more than 15% above 110
Accept them, since fuse resistance is not measured on network protectors
Replace all three
explanation: ATS has you measure each network protector power fuse and investigate values that differ from each other by more than 15%. (128 − 110) / 110 is about 16%, so it gets investigated. The 50% rule is for bolted connections. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.8.B.6 and D.6.

question: A low-voltage power circuit breaker's enclosure always stays well below 40 °C. Per IEEE C37.13-2015, what does that mean for its current rating?
choices: Nothing; the rating is fixed
It may carry more than its continuous rating, but life and long-time performance can suffer, so check with the manufacturer
It must be derated
It can carry 125% indefinitely
explanation: Below a 40 °C ambient the breaker may be able to carry current above its continuous rating. Because that can affect long-time performance and useful life, consult the manufacturer about any added capability, and re-evaluate trip-device settings. Source: IEEE C37.13-2015, A.1.3.3.

question: You're running an inverse-time trip test on a three-pole thermal-magnetic molded-case breaker per NEMA AB 4-2017. How is the test set up?
choices: All three poles in series at 150% current
One pole at a time at 300% of rated current, with copper leads at least 4 ft long, in about a 25 °C room
All poles in parallel at 300% current
One pole at 1000% current to check the instantaneous
explanation: Test each pole individually at 300% of rated current; that current is easy to reach and keeps heat transfer into adjacent poles small. Connect with copper conductors at least 4 ft (1.2 m) long sized per Table 1, at roughly 25 °C ambient. Electronic trip units with ground-fault protection are tested with two or more poles in series. ATS Table 100.7 is derived from AB 4 Table 3. Source: NEMA AB 4-2017, 6.5.4.
reference: NEMA AB 4-2017, 6.5.4; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.7 note 1

question: A network protector has a submersible enclosure. ATS 7.8 calls for:
choices: A leak test, per the manufacturer
A vacuum-bottle magnetron test
An SF6 moisture sample
A 5 kV jacket test of the enclosure
explanation: Submersible protectors sit in vaults that can flood, so the enclosure's seal is checked with a leak test using the manufacturer's method. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.8.A.17.

question: A network protector's rated control voltage is 120 V. Its motor control relay picks up at 96 V. Under ATS 7.8:
choices: Accept, because 96 V is within 80% of rated
Accept, because pickup only has to be below rated control voltage
Investigate; the limit is 90 V (75%)
Investigate, because pickup must be below 60 V
explanation: ATS requires the motor control relay to pick up at no more than 75% of rated control voltage: 0.75 x 120 = 90 V. The motor and trip actuator have the same 75% criterion. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.8.B.7 and D.7.

question: A short circuit occurs on a primary feeder that supplies one of several network transformers. Per IEEE C37.108, what usually happens next?
choices: The protectors open first, then the feeder breaker
The whole network drops until the feeder is repaired
Feeder breaker trips, then protectors open on reverse power; the network stays up
The protectors open first on overcurrent, then the feeder breaker trips and the network drops
explanation: Operation is sequential. The substation feeder breaker clears, then each network master relay sees reverse power (transformer magnetizing and feeder load) and opens its protector. Other feeders carry the network, so customers don't lose service. Source: IEEE C37.108-2021, 5.1.

question: On an electromechanical network protector, what does the phasing relay add to the master relay's closing logic?
choices: It permits closing only when transformer voltage leads the network
It trips the protector on any forward power
It closes the protector whenever the network voltage leads the transformer voltage
It blocks tripping when the feeder breaker is open
explanation: The master relay holds the trip and close functions. The phasing relay supervises closing so the protector closes only when the transformer side leads the network, which means power will flow into the network. Source: IEEE C37.108-2021, 6.1.5.

question: An arcing fault develops inside a network protector enclosure. Per IEEE C37.108, why might the network master relay not clear it?
choices: The master relay has no current inputs
The master relay only trips on undervoltage
The master relay is blocked whenever the feeder breaker is still closed at the substation
It is directional, and that fault doesn't look like reverse power to it
explanation: The master relay responds to power flowing back toward the transformer. A fault inside the protector isn't seen that way and may burn until the primary feeder relays finally see it. Source: IEEE C37.108-2021, 5.2.3.

question: You read a low-voltage power breaker's operations counter, run one close-open cycle, and read it again. Per ATS 7.6.1.2, a good counter:
choices: Advanced two counts, one for close and one for open
Advanced exactly one count
Didn't move, since the counter only logs trips
Reset to zero after the cycle
explanation: ATS has you record the as-found and as-left counter readings. The test value is that the counter advances one digit per close-open cycle. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.A.15 and C.4.

question: Which pair of items is in the ATS 7.6.1.2 visual and mechanical list for a drawout low-voltage power breaker?
choices: Contact resistance and insulation resistance
Cell fit and element alignment, and racking mechanism operation
Primary injection of long-time and short-time
Trip-unit battery condition and zone interlocking
explanation: Cell fit, element alignment, and racking operation are mechanical checks in part A. Contact and insulation resistance, the injection tests, and the auxiliary-feature checks (battery, zone interlocking) are electrical tests in part B. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.A.11, A.12, and B.1–B.8.

question: A 480 V power breaker has no manufacturer insulation-test data. What does the ATS 7.6.1.2 test look like?
choices: Ten minutes phase-to-ground only, at 500 V dc with 25 MΩ minimum
One minute across open poles only, at 2500 V dc
One minute at 5000 V dc, phase-to-phase only
One minute, each pole phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground closed and across each open pole, at 1000 V dc with 100 MΩ as the minimum
explanation: B.1 covers closed (phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground) and open (across each pole) connections for one minute. With no manufacturer data, Table 100.1 for 600 V equipment gives 1000 V dc and a 100 MΩ minimum at 20 °C. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.1; Table 100.1.

question: After primary injection on a low-voltage power breaker is finished, ATS 7.6.1.2 tells you to:
choices: Reset all trip logs and indicators
Leave the trip targets showing for the owner
Clear only the ground-fault target
Remove the trip-unit battery to clear memory
explanation: The last step of B.8, after verifying auxiliary features, is to reset trip logs and indicators. A breaker that goes back in service with old targets showing will confuse the next person who reads them after a real trip. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8.

question: ATS 7.6.1.2 lists 'verify operation of charging mechanism' as an electrical test. What is the result judged against?
choices: Table 100.20 control voltage limits only
A fixed recharge time of 10 seconds
The manufacturer's published data
The coordination study
explanation: B.9 checks the spring-charging mechanism, and D.10 says it shall operate per the manufacturer's published data. ATS gives no generic recharge time. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.9 and D.10.

question: What does an energy-reducing maintenance switch (maintenance mode) on a breaker trip unit do?
choices: Opens the breaker so the gear is de-energized for maintenance
Raises the instantaneous pickup to stop nuisance trips during work
Temporarily sets the trip unit to operate faster while someone works inside the arc flash boundary, then goes back to normal
Bypasses the trip unit so the breaker can't trip during testing
explanation: NFPA 70E's design annex lists energy-reducing maintenance switching with a local status indicator as an incident-energy reduction method. It speeds up tripping during the work and is set back to normal afterward. The gear stays energized. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, Informative Annex O, O.2.3(3).

question: Why does making a breaker trip faster lower the arc-flash incident energy downstream of it?
choices: Incident energy rises roughly in proportion to arc duration, so shorter clearing time means less energy
Faster tripping lowers the available fault current
It raises the arcing voltage, which shortens the arc
It reduces the working distance
explanation: The IEEE 1584 test program concluded that arc duration has a linear effect on incident energy. Cutting the clearing time by half cuts the energy roughly in half. Available fault current and working distance don't change. Source: IEEE 1584-2018, Annex G.3 a).

question: A main breaker's maintenance mode is left ON after work is done. A fault on a downstream feeder exceeds the maintenance pickup. What is likely?
choices: Nothing changes, since maintenance mode only acts on faults inside the main's own cubicle
The feeder breaker is forced to trip faster
The main locks out and won't trip at all
The main trips with no intentional delay, taking out the whole bus instead of only the feeder
explanation: In maintenance mode the trip unit trips with no intentional delay whenever the set pickup is exceeded, regardless of the normal instantaneous setting. That defeats the time separation the coordination study relied on. Turn it off and confirm the indicator when the work ends. Source: Eaton MN013003EN, PXR 20/25 Trip Unit for Series NRX User Manual, 4.6.
reference: Eaton MN013003EN, PXR 20/25 Trip Unit for Series NRX User Manual, 4.6

question: On an Eaton PXR trip unit with the ARMS (maintenance mode) switch, how can you tell maintenance mode is active?
choices: The LONG pickup LED flashes
A blue ring around the maintenance switch lights
The breaker's spring-charge flag turns yellow
The display shows only the ground-fault setting
explanation: The PXR manual says a blue ring around the maintenance mode switch always lights to confirm the function is enabled. There's also an optional normally open contact for remote indication. Source: Eaton MN013003EN, PXR 20/25 Trip Unit for Series NRX User Manual, 3.5 and 4.6.1.
reference: Eaton MN013003EN, PXR 20/25 Trip Unit for Series NRX User Manual, 3.5 and 4.6.1

question: On a PXR trip unit, maintenance mode was turned on through communications software. A tech flips the front switch to ON and back to OFF/Remote. What is the result?
choices: Maintenance mode turns off
Maintenance mode stays on; it has to be turned off through communications
The trip unit resets to factory settings
The breaker trips to confirm the change
explanation: The manual says that when maintenance mode is enabled remotely or over communications it must also be disabled the same way. Cycling the local switch does not disable it. Check the blue indicator before you leave. Source: Eaton MN013003EN, PXR 20/25 Trip Unit for Series NRX User Manual, 4.6.1.
reference: Eaton MN013003EN, PXR 20/25 Trip Unit for Series NRX User Manual, 4.6.1

question: A relay-based arc energy reduction scheme uses a maintenance setting group and light sensors. ATS-2025 7.27 is marked reserved. Where do the acceptance checks come from?
choices: Nowhere, so the scheme is accepted untested
7.6.1.1 molded-case breakers
Table 100.8 instantaneous tolerances only
The microprocessor relay section, 7.9.2.B.6, which includes verifying logic for normal and maintenance modes
explanation: ATS 7.9.2.B.6 lists arc energy reduction items: pickup and timing of the elements used, zone interlocking, normal versus maintenance mode logic, communication-failure alarms, light-sensor ambient and pickup, and current supervision. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.B.6 and 7.27.

question: An incident energy analysis assumed a feeder breaker clears in its normal time. The breaker hasn't been exercised in years and now trips slowly. Under NFPA 70E, why does that matter?
choices: The analysis must account for the device's clearing time including its condition of maintenance, so the label may understate the hazard
It doesn't, since labels are based on available fault current only
Only the arc flash boundary changes, not the incident energy
A slow breaker lowers incident energy
explanation: 70E 130.5(G) requires the incident energy analysis to consider the overcurrent device's characteristics and clearing time, including its condition of maintenance. Longer clearing time means more incident energy than the label shows. Source: NFPA 70E-2024, 130.5(G).
